questions.title: How does the entropy-based patching algorithm decide where to split a byte sequence?
questions.question_body: In the Byte Latent Transformer paper, they introduce two entropy‑based patching constraints: a global threshold ($H(x_t) > 	heta_g$) and an approximate monotonic constraint ($H(x_t) - H(x_{t-1}) > 	heta_r$). I understand that $H(x_i)$ is the entropy of the next‑byte prediction from a small byte LM, but I’m unclear on how these thresholds are applied in practice. For instance, if a sequence starts with bytes of consistently low entropy, does the algorithm wait until the monotonic increase triggers a patch boundary? Also, how are the values of $	heta_g$ and $	heta_r$ chosen—do they depend on desired average patch size or something else?

questions.title: What exactly makes a patching scheme "incremental" and why can BPE not be considered incremental?
questions.question_body: The paper states that an incremental patching scheme satisfies $f_p( m{x}_{<i}) = f_p( m{x})_{<i}$ and claims that BPE fails this property because the same prefix can be tokenized differently depending on the rest of the sequence. Could someone provide a concrete example where tokenizing a prefix with BPE gives different tokens based on future bytes? Additionally, how would adding a special delimiter token turn BPE into an incremental scheme, and why is this not ideal for byte‑level models?

questions.title: Why does the Local Encoder use cross‑attention instead of just pooling byte representations?
questions.question_body: In Section 4.2.2 (Encoder Multi‑Headed Cross‑Attention), the authors say they add a cross‑attention block after each transformer layer to pool byte representations into patch representations. What is the benefit of having this cross‑attention at every layer rather than simply applying a single pooling operation after the final encoder layer? Does it help model interactions between bytes inside a patch or enable dynamic representation merging as more context is processed?

questions.title: How are bits‑per‑byte (BPB) values comparable across different tokenization setups?
questions.question_body: The paper reports BPB rather than perplexity to compare byte‑level and token‑level models. Since BPB normalizes by number of bytes and logarithm base 2, how should we interpret identical BPB between two models that use very different vocabularies? For example, if a tokenized model has a 128K vocabulary versus a byte model with no vocabulary, do low BPB scores necessarily indicate better compression or just less learned parameters per byte?

questions.title: What role do n‑gram hash embeddings play in improving BLT’s performance?
questions.question_body: Section 4.2.1 mentions adding hash n‑gram embeddings for n=3…8 to each byte input. I’m unsure whether these embeddings are used only during training or also at inference time. How much do they contribute compared to cross‑attention? The ablation results suggest diminishing returns beyond 300K hashes; could you explain why increasing hash table size stalls performance gains?

questions.title: Why does BLT‘s scaling trend improve when both model size and patch size grow simultaneously?
questions.question_body: "Patches Scale Better Than Tokens" claims that increasing patch size while increasing model size yields better scaling than token‑based models at fixed inference cost. Mechanistically, how does longer average patch size reduce flops for global transformer steps? Also, why does this design allow us to reallocate compute to grow the latent transformer without affecting local encoder/decoder costs?

questions.title: "Entropy Model Context" – When should we reset its context during training?
questions.question_body: The authors mention resetting the entropy context with new lines for large‐scale runs to avoid 'entropy drift'. Under what conditions does context carry over from one sample to another affect entropy estimates? Is the reset done per training example or per batch? How sensitive is BLT’s performance to this design choice?

questions.title: "Bagging layers": Why use more decoder layers than encoder layers in BLT’s local modules?
questions.question_body: In Table A (local_layers ablation), it's shown that using only one encoder layer but several decoder layers works well with hash embeddings. Intuitively I'd expect symmetry between encoding and decoding—why is it beneficial for the decoder to be heavier than the encoder in BLT?

questions.title: `f_p` under random whitespace characters – potential issues
questions.question_body: 'Space Patching' creates new patches after any space-like byte (non-Latin character). In languages with many punctuation marks or scripts that lack clear space separators (e.g., Chinese), could this strategy lead to highly variable patch sizes or even extremely long patches? How does BLT handle such cases given that dynamic entropy‐based patching can adapt patch lengths?

questions.title: Computational cost breakdown – why do local encoder/decoder flops appear small compared with global transformer flops?
questions.question_body: "FL_psc" equation shows terms like Transf.FL(h_G,l_G,m=n_ctx/n_p). The local encoder has small window sizes (w_E). In practice, what proportion of total flops during inference comes from encoder versus global transformer when using large patches? Does this proportion shift dramatically as we increase model depth l_G?

questions.title: $S_0$ initialization for cross-attention queries in Local Encoder
questions.question_body: "The scheme initializes queries for first cross-attention by max-pooling over pixel representations"—I’d like clarification: what exactly gets pooled? Do we pool over all bytes in each patch before feeding them into cross-attention? Is there any positional information left after pooling, and if not, why does this design still work well?
